section.title: The Marriage of the Lamb
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 18 ended with the great prostitute Babylon in ashes and the merchants of the earth weeping over her ruin. Chapter 19 opens the seam: heaven itself answers with a fourfold Hallelujah, the only four times that word appears in the whole New Testament, and the scene pivots from a judged prostitute to a prepared bride. The unit closes when John, overwhelmed, falls to worship the revealing angel and is firmly redirected to God alone, a clean hinge before the rider on the white horse appears in the next scene.
section.thesis: Heaven answers the fall of Babylon with an outburst of praise, then announces the wedding the whole story of Scripture has been moving toward: the Lamb takes His bride, clothed not in her own achievement but in the righteous acts He gives her to do, and even the angel who announces it insists that God alone is to be worshiped.
section.frameNote: Five beats: heaven's fourfold Hallelujah over Babylon's judgment; the voice from the throne calling every servant of God to praise; the announcement of the marriage of the Lamb and the bride made ready; the beatitude on those invited to the supper; and the angel's refusal of worship, pointing every eye back to God.

units.label: Heaven's Hallelujah
units.note: praise for the judgment of the prostitute

verses.text: After this I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude in heaven, shouting: “{{allelouia|Hallelujah}}! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!
For His judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand.”
And a second time they called out: “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.”
And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne, saying: “Amen, Hallelujah!”

units.label: Praise our God, small and great

verses.text: Then a voice came from the throne, saying: “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!”
And I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude, like the rushing of many waters, and like a mighty rumbling of thunder, crying out: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.
Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the {{gamos|marriage}} of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready.
She was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure.” For the fine linen she wears is the {{dikaiomata|righteous acts}} of the saints.
Then the angel told me to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he said to me, “These are the true words of God.”

So I fell at his feet to {{proskyneo|worship}} him. But he told me, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the {{martyria|testimony}} of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.”

allelouia.gloss: Hallelujah, a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew hallelu Yah, praise the LORD. It occurs only here in the entire New Testament, four times in six verses, as heaven bursts into praise over the judgment of Babylon and the coming marriage of the Lamb.

gamos.gloss: Marriage or wedding. Scripture has long pictured God's covenant with His people as a marriage; here the picture reaches its resolution as the Lamb's wedding day arrives and His bride, the redeemed, is finally and fully joined to Him.

dikaiomata.gloss: Righteous acts or righteous deeds, the plural of dikaioma. Distinct from dikaiosyne, the righteousness credited to believers by faith, this word names the actual good deeds the saints do, deeds the text says the bride is given to wear, grace producing genuine fruit.

martyria.gloss: Testimony or witness. The testimony of Jesus, held by His people even to death, is here called the spirit of prophecy, the animating center of every true prophetic word, gathering the whole book of Revelation around the witness to Christ.

proskyneo.gloss: To worship, literally to fall down and kiss toward, an act of prostration and homage. John instinctively offers it to the dazzling angel; the angel's sharp refusal, twice repeated in Revelation, insists that this act belongs to God alone.

basic.context: Babylon, the great prostitute, has just fallen in chapter 18. Now heaven erupts in a fourfold shout of Hallelujah, praising God for judging her truly and justly. Then the scene turns joyful: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride, the redeemed people of God, is dressed not in her own effort but in righteous acts she is given to wear. An angel pronounces those invited to the wedding supper blessed, and when John falls down to worship him, the angel refuses, insisting worship belongs to God alone.
basic.hermeneutics: This scene answers Babylon's fall with heaven's praise and turns immediately to a wedding, a deliberate contrast the whole chapter is built on. Readers debate exactly who the bride is, the church, the true Israel, or both together, and whether the bride's fine linen is purely a gift or also the visible fruit of a transformed life; Scripture holds both together, grace that produces real, good works. What is not in doubt is the center: judgment falls, joy rises, and every impulse to worship anyone but God is refused.
basic.originalLanguages: Four times the word allelouia rings out, hallelu Yah, the only place it appears in the whole New Testament. The gamos, the marriage, of the Lamb has come, and the bride wears the dikaiomata, the righteous acts, of the saints, given to her rather than woven by her own hands. When John tries to proskyneo, worship, the angel who bears the martyria, the testimony, of Jesus, he is refused and pointed back to God.
basic.typology: The marriage supper of the Lamb fulfills a long biblical pattern, God as bridegroom and His people as bride, running from the prophets' pictures of Israel's unfaithfulness to Paul's teaching that marriage itself is a picture of Christ and the church. The bride's fine linen, given rather than self-woven, points to a righteousness that is first received before it is lived out.
basic.christ: This is the Lamb's wedding day, the goal toward which the whole story of Scripture has been moving. The Bridegroom who was slain has judged the prostitute who corrupted the earth and now takes to Himself a bride made ready, not by her own effort, but by what He gives her to wear. His testimony is called the spirit of all true prophecy, the center that every word from God finally points to.
basic.god: God is praised as true and just in judgment, and as the one whose reign is the ground of all rejoicing, small and great alike are called to praise Him. When an overwhelmed John tries to worship the angel instead, the angel's sharp refusal protects what matters most in this whole scene, that worship belongs to God and to Him only.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah, Hosea, and Ezekiel all picture God's covenant with His people as a marriage, often a strained one. Ephesians 5 teaches that human marriage itself pictures Christ and the church. And Revelation 22 later repeats the same refusal of worship offered to an angel, showing this is not a one time slip but a settled pattern in the book.
basic.oneStory: The story that began with a bride corrupted by unfaithfulness in the prophets now ends with a bride made ready, clothed in righteous acts she did not weave herself. Babylon's judgment and the Lamb's wedding are two sides of the same turning point, and the scene closes by insisting that every ounce of the glory, and the worship, belongs to God alone.

context.literary:
The ten verses fall into four movements that climb in volume and then deliberately drop. First comes a shout of praise for judgment, verses 1 to 3, in two bursts that each begin with the same cry. Then the worship moves inward to the throne, where the elders and living creatures answer with 'Amen, Hallelujah,' verse 4, and a voice from the throne widens the circle to all who serve God, verse 5. The third movement is the loudest, a sound like rushing water and thunder, verses 6 to 8, and its content turns from the verdict on Babylon to a new announcement, the wedding. The last movement, verses 9 and 10, is quieter, a conversation between John and an angel, with a command to write and a refusal of worship.

Look at the way the chapter hinges. The first word of verse 1 is 'After this,' and the multitude's first subject is the destruction just recorded in chapter 18, so the great prostitute is judged inside the very same sentence that announces the bride's readiness. Babylon is mentioned for the last time in verse 2 and the bride appears for the first in verse 7. The reader is walked directly from the harlot's smoke to the wedding clothes.

Notice also the unusual structure of the speech. The multitude's cry in verse 7 is a three part call, 'rejoice,' 'be glad,' 'give Him the glory,' followed by two reasons joined by 'for.' It is hymn style, and the parallelism between the praise for judgment in verse 2 and the praise for marriage in verse 7 makes them one act. Justice and joy are two sides of the same reign.

The scene closes with a small drama of its own. John falls and is stopped, verse 10, and the near mirror in Revelation 22:8 and 22:9 frames the book's last part with the same refusal. These two scenes form a pair of bookends around the final visions, and each time the angel says, 'Worship God!'
context.historical:
A first century wedding moved in three stages that help unlock verses 7 to 9. First came the betrothal, a binding agreement in which the couple were already legally pledged, as with Mary and Joseph, Matthew 1:18 and 1:19. Then, often a year or more later, the groom came for the bride in a procession, the very scene of the ten virgins who waited with lamps, Matthew 25:1 to 10. Finally came the wedding feast at the groom's house, sometimes lasting days. The book of Revelation places believers in the interval. They are betrothed, as Paul says, 'I promised you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ,' 2 Corinthians 11:2, and now the groom has come and the feast begins.

The shout of 'Hallelujah' belongs to Israel's temple worship. The Hebrew phrase appears at the head or the close of a series of psalms, Psalms 113 to 118 and 146 to 150, and the Jews sang the Psalms of the Hallel at Passover and the great feasts. The multitude's cry therefore sounds like a festival procession, with the heavenly crowd taking up the liturgy of Jerusalem. After the Roman war that destroyed the temple, the shout would feel like the return of public worship to a people with no sanctuary.

The refusal of worship would also have had pointed meaning. Emperors, and in the east their governors and local benefactors, were honoured with prostration, and the imperial cult was the empire's test of loyalty. John, a servant of the king of kings, kneels at the wrong feet and is stopped. The angel's reply reminds a Roman world that no creature, however high, may receive the worship that belongs to God.

Lastly, the 'fine linen, bright and pure' in verse 8 contrasts with the clothes in chapter 17 and 18, where the harlot wears purple, scarlet and gold. Linen was the textile of priests, Exodus 28:39 and Leviticus 16:4, and of Egypt's trade. The clothing in verse 8 is a priestly, simple, white garment, and it would have been read as the opposite of the empire's display.
context.canonical:
The wedding is the oldest image of God's relation to His people, and chapter 19 gathers every strand of it. The prophets said that the LORD had betrothed Israel to Himself, Hosea 2:19 and 2:20, that He rejoices over her as a bridegroom over his bride, Isaiah 62:5, and that her Maker was her husband, Isaiah 54:5. They also said she had played the harlot, which is why Revelation can set the faithless city beside the faithful one. The Song of Songs belongs to the same ground, and Psalm 45 sings a royal wedding.

The New Testament carries the image onto Jesus. John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom who rejoices to hear his voice, John 3:29. Jesus compares the kingdom to a wedding banquet for the king's son, Matthew 22:2, and calls Himself the bridegroom whose guests cannot fast while He is with them, Mark 2:19. Paul says that Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her 'to sanctify her,' to present her without stain, Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and he calls marriage itself a profound mystery pointing to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:32.

Within Revelation the marriage language is prepared early. The faithful in Sardis are promised white garments, Revelation 3:4 and 3:5, and the faithless in Laodicea are counselled to buy white garments so that their shameful nakedness will not be seen, Revelation 3:18. The great multitude of chapter 7 has 'washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb,' Revelation 7:14. These threads tie into verse 8. The bride's clothing is not a new theme but the end of an old one.

The refusal of worship ties forward to Revelation 22:8 and 22:9 and backward to Acts 10:25 and 10:26, where Peter lifts up Cornelius. The beatitude in verse 9 is the fourth of seven in the book, beginning at Revelation 1:3 and ending at 22:14. The book proposes seven times that blessing is for those who keep what is written, and the guests of the marriage supper are among them.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wanted to give believers who stood in the shadow of Babylon the one thing they could not see: the sound of what is waiting for them. Persecuted people need more than a promise that their enemy will be punished. They need to hear that someone is celebrating and that they have a place in the celebration. The chapter opens with the loudest worship in the book and ends with a blessing that is addressed to them personally. The 'Blessed are those who are invited' is a pastoral sentence to churches who feared they would be left out.

He also wants the reader to hear the praise as moral. The multitude does not first rejoice that their enemies are dead. They rejoice that God's judgments are 'true and just,' verse 2. Justice is the ground of joy. Believers who have watched evil win for a long time are taught that their longing for justice is not unholy, because heaven shares it.

The bride's clothing is meant to be received with gratitude and responsibility. 'She was given' stops any boasting, and 'the righteous acts of the saints' stops any idea that the life of faith is a waiting room. John's readers had been told they would need to endure, and he adds that endurance and faithfulness are exactly what the wedding dress is made of.

Finally, the scene is a guard rail. John himself is overwhelmed and kneels to the wrong person, and the angel's rebuke teaches the church that the greatness of a revelation never makes the messenger worthy of worship.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the passage describes what heaven says and does. The singing is a report of what happens in heaven and invites, rather than commands, an earthly echo, though verse 5 gives a plain instruction: 'Praise our God, all you who serve Him.' The command to write in verse 9 was for John alone, but the beatitude he writes holds for every reader.

The marriage image is a description of the future and a picture of the present relationship. It does not prescribe a particular practice of marriage, and the verse where the bride 'made herself ready' should not be turned into a recipe for earning a place. Nor should it be taken as a tool for pressing every person into one marriage framework. Paul uses the same image for the church in Ephesians 5, while also warning that its reality lies in Christ. The wedding clothes are the closest thing to a demand, and they ask for the kind of life described in Ephesians 2:10, good works God prepared in advance, within a salvation that is a gift, Ephesians 2:8 and 2:9.

The angel's refusal is the clearest prescription. Worship is reserved for God, and no vision, angel, saint, preacher or institution may be given it. That is a rule for the church in any age, and it explains why Revelation repeats it at the end of the book, Revelation 22:9.

debates.question: Who is the bride, and who are the guests?

views.label: The church, universal and complete
views.case: The bride is the whole people of God redeemed in Christ, and Revelation 21:9 and 21:10 identifies the bride with the New Jerusalem, a city that includes the names of the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles, Revelation 21:12 to 14. The guests in verse 9 are the same people seen from another angle, the way a man may speak of the church both as his body and as his bride. This is the majority reading in church history and fits Ephesians 5:25 to 32.

views.label: The church as bride and Old Testament saints as guests
views.case: Some dispensational readers see a distinction. The bride is the church of this age, which is joined to Christ at His coming, while Old Testament saints and tribulation saints are the guests called to the supper. They point to the wedding feast language of verse 9 as distinct from the bride's own dress in verse 8, and to John the Baptist calling himself a friend of the bridegroom, John 3:29.

views.label: Both are one people described by two images
views.case: Others hold that bride and guests are two metaphors for one people. Scripture happily mixes pictures, as in Revelation 21:2, where the city is dressed as a bride, and in Matthew 22 where the same people are guests. This reading finds the bride and the invited together as the covenant people of every age.

debates.bearing: The disagreement is about the shape of the redeemed community, not about whether they are blessed. All three views agree that the invitation is real, that those who come are clothed by Christ, and that the supper is the joy of His whole people. A reader can enjoy the scene without settling the question.

debates.question: What does 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy' mean?

views.label: The testimony Jesus bore
views.case: On this reading 'of Jesus' is a subjective genitive: the testimony given by Jesus Himself. Prophecy is the Spirit's work of bearing witness for Him. Revelation 1:2 calls the whole book 'the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ,' and 1:5 calls Him 'the faithful witness,' which supports reading the phrase as what He says and shows.

views.label: The testimony about Jesus
views.case: Others read an objective genitive: the witness that people bear to Jesus. The saints 'hold to the testimony of Jesus,' Revelation 12:17, and the martyrs died for it. On this view prophecy is not an independent source of revelation but the Spirit empowering the church to confess Christ. The angel's own claim, 'a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus,' fits this.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many interpreters hold that the grammar is deliberately open. Jesus bears witness through His Spirit, and His people bear witness to Him, and the two cannot be separated. The testimony that came from Him becomes the testimony the church carries.

debates.bearing: All three views agree on the main point of the sentence: true prophecy has Jesus at its centre, and that is why the angel cannot be worshiped. Whatever grammar one chooses, prophecy is a servant of the testimony to Christ rather than its rival.

study.originalLanguages:
The phrase translated 'the Lord our God the Almighty reigns' in verse 6 has a surprising tense. The verb ebasileusen is an aorist, which in this setting is best understood as 'has begun to reign' or 'has taken up His reign.' Revelation 11:17 uses the same form when the elders say, 'You have taken Your great power and have begun to reign.' The Greek for Almighty, pantokrator, is the book's favourite title for God, used in Revelation 1:8, 4:8, 11:17, 15:3 and 16:7, and in the New Testament outside Revelation only in 2 Corinthians 6:18. It carries the sense of ruler of all things, and the Septuagint uses it for the Hebrew 'LORD of Hosts.' The word marks the song as a reply to every claimant who said, 'Caesar is lord.'

The bride in verse 7 is, literally, 'His wife,' gyne. The Greek has a perfectly good word for 'bride,' nymphe, and John uses it in Revelation 21:2 and 22:17, but in 19:7 and 21:9 he says 'wife.' The bride in this scene is the covenant partner in the full sense, with the status of a married woman, even though the feast is only beginning. The two words together, bride and wife, show a relationship already settled and still being consummated, which is the situation of the church.

Her preparation is carefully worded. 'Has made herself ready,' hetoimasen heauten, is active, so she took part. But the clothing 'was given' to her, edothe autei, a divine passive that makes God the giver. The sentence therefore holds both sides in one frame: she prepared, and she received. The clothing itself is byssinon, fine linen, the same material that Babylon wore in Revelation 18:16. The same fabric, two different wearers, and the difference is where it came from.

The word translated 'supper,' deipnon, was the main evening meal, the feast of the day. It returns in Revelation 19:17, where the angel calls birds to 'the great supper of God.' The same word names both feasts. One table is set for those clothed in linen and the other for the carrion birds, and the reader learns that every person ends at one table or the other.

The word 'blessed,' makarios, opens the fourth of seven beatitudes in Revelation, 1:3, 14:13, 16:15, 19:9, 20:6, 22:7 and 22:14. The word describes a settled state of favour, not a passing feeling. The invitation list is declared blessed before anyone has yet sat down.

Last, the fellowship phrase 'fellow servant,' syndoulos, which the angel uses in verse 10, puts John and the angel side by side in the household of the same master. Rank is not abolished, since the angel is the messenger, but status before God is shared. The same word returns in Revelation 22:9, and in 6:11 it names the 'fellow servants' of the martyrs still to come.

typology.type: The wedding of the LORD and His people
typology.fulfillment: The marriage of God and Israel runs from Hosea 2:19 to Isaiah 62:5, where He rejoices over her as a bridegroom over a bride. The pattern is also marked by pain, since Ezekiel 16 shows the groom who clothes the bride in fine linen and adorns her, and the bride who then turns to harlotry. In Christ the story is not abandoned but finished. The bridegroom comes in person, John 3:29, and pays the price of her purification, Ephesians 5:25 to 27. The type falls short because earthly marriages end in death, while this marriage is the one that sets all others in their light, and the wedding supper, unlike earthly feasts, has no last course.

Joshua the high priest stood in filthy garments until the angel said, 'See, I have removed your iniquity, and I will clothe you with splendid robes,' Zechariah 3:4. Isaiah says, 'He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness,' Isaiah 61:10, and he places it in a wedding picture. In Revelation 19:8 the linen is given, and its threads are 'the righteous acts of the saints.' Christ is the escalation: in Him believers are clothed, Galatians 3:27, and then grow into what they have put on, Colossians 3:12. The earlier types point to a covering for a single priest or single moment; here the covering is the shared garment of a whole people.

Isaiah 25:6 to 8 promises a banquet on the mountain for all peoples, in which God swallows up death and wipes away tears. The Passover meal and the feasts of Israel pointed ahead to such a table, and at the Last Supper Jesus said that He would not drink the fruit of the vine again 'until the kingdom of God comes,' Luke 22:18. Revelation 19:9 is that table. The Lord's Supper looks backward to the cross and forward to this feast, 1 Corinthians 11:26. The type falls short because the earlier tables were shared by a gathering of the covenant people in one place, whereas this feast gathers a multitude from every nation, Revelation 7:9.

Peter lifts up Cornelius, Acts 10:25 and 10:26, and Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes when a crowd calls them gods, Acts 14:14 and 14:15. The pattern of faithful servants refusing worship runs through the Bible and ends in the angel's rebuke. Christ stands in contrast, since He receives worship without protest, Matthew 14:33 and John 20:28, and His acceptance is one of the strongest signs of His deity. The type is incomplete in that no creature can complete the pattern; only the Son can receive what the angel must refuse.

study.christ:
Christ is named at the end of the passage, in the angel's statement that 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy,' but He is present in nearly every phrase. The central figure of the wedding is 'the Lamb,' the title the book gave Him at the throne in Revelation 5:6. The Lamb who was slain is now the bridegroom. The same blood that bought the bride's freedom pays for her wedding. The title ties the wedding to the cross in the most direct way: the Lamb gets His bride by dying for her.

The passage fulfils what Jesus said about Himself in the Gospels. He called Himself the bridegroom, Mark 2:19, told parables of wedding feasts that He Himself would host, Matthew 22:2 and 25:10, and promised at His last Passover that He would not drink the cup again 'until the kingdom of God comes,' Luke 22:18. The wedding supper of Revelation 19 is the fulfilment of that promise, the day His table is set again.

The bride's clothing shows how Christ's work and ours fit. 'It was given' points to the gift: He is the one who 'has released us from our sins by His blood,' Revelation 1:5, and who counsels the poor to buy white garments from Him, Revelation 3:18. 'The righteous acts of the saints' points to the life that grows from that gift, which is what Paul meant when he wrote that we are 'created in Christ Jesus to do good works,' Ephesians 2:10. Christ both clothes and transforms. A reader who looks only at the gift forgets Christ the Lord; a reader who looks only at the acts forgets Christ the Saviour.

The refusal of worship in verse 10 sheds an indirect light on Jesus. The angel says, 'Worship God!' yet throughout Revelation the Lamb receives worship, Revelation 5:8 to 14, and the twenty four elders and the whole creation give Him the praise that belongs to God. Either the book contradicts itself or it is teaching that the Lamb is God. The angel's rebuke is a quiet proof that the worship offered to Christ is the worship of God.

Finally, the verse 10 statement links Christ to prophecy as a whole. If His testimony is the soul of prophecy, then every prophet from Moses on was speaking about Him, as He told two disciples on the Emmaus road, Luke 24:27. Prophecy ends where it began, with a person, not a timetable.

The caution is that the passage's wedding imagery is a picture. It does not mean that Christ's relationship to His people is a romantic feeling or that the church is a bride in a literal sense. The image conveys covenant love, faithfulness, purity and joy, and it must not be pushed into detail the text does not give.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He is the one who speaks in justice and receives praise for it. The multitude does not say 'Salvation and glory and power belong to our God' after a vague hope. They say it because 'His judgments are true and just,' verse 2. In Scripture the truthfulness of God is bound up with His verdicts. Abraham's question, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25, is answered here in a thunder of yes. God is not tempted to bend a sentence in favour of the powerful, and He is not too soft to condemn what has wrecked the earth.

He is the God who reigns, and the verb marks a decisive moment. 'The Lord our God the Almighty reigns,' verse 6, is a statement about divine sovereignty that does not wait for the last enemy to fall. His power is not shown by thrashing out a contest but by an arrival. His people are shown seeing the present rule of God from the inside of heaven. For worship this means that the church is not asking God to begin to reign. It is giving Him glory because He does.

He is a God who marries. This is among the most daring things Scripture says of Him. He does not only rule, judge or save, He binds Himself to His people in covenant love. The prophets said He would be a husband to them, Isaiah 54:5, and that He would rejoice over them, Isaiah 62:5. Here the Lamb's wedding is the end of that long courtship. God's holiness and His desire are not rivals. The same God who burns Babylon rejoices over His bride.

He is generous in a way that humbles. The clothes are 'given.' The invitation is a blessing. Nothing in the scene leaves room for merit. The supper is paid for, the guests are called, the garment is supplied, and then they are praised for wearing it. Such grace does not remove responsibility, as the bride 'made herself ready,' but it ensures that no one can boast, Ephesians 2:9.

He is jealous for His own glory, and the angel's refusal shows it. 'Worship God!' states that worship is the one thing God does not share, Isaiah 42:8. Yet He is not selfish, for the God who claims all worship also includes His servants in the feast, calling them 'small and great alike,' verse 5. The same God who forbids worship of a creature invites creatures to His table.

He is also a God of fixed outcomes. 'Her smoke rises forever and ever,' verse 3, tells us the verdict will not be reversed. Believers who have prayed for justice for years are shown that the case is closed and that no appeal remains.

For worship, the lesson is to learn the whole range of the multitude's response: gladness at justice, amazement at grace, and fear of the Lord. The praise is not ours to produce, but it is ours to join.

crossReferences.note: The great prostitute is introduced here, drunk with the blood of the saints and dressed in purple and scarlet. Chapter 19 begins by celebrating her judgment and moves to the bride, so the two women are intended to be read together, one false and fatal and the other faithful and clothed by the Lamb.

The voice of bride and bridegroom will never be heard in Babylon again. The verse is answered in chapter 19, where a different wedding is announced. What the city lost, joy and companionship, the faithful receive in full, and the silence of the harlot's streets is replaced by the noise of heaven.

The Hallel psalms open with the same cry used in Revelation 19:1. In Jewish worship these were sung at Passover, so the multitude's shout carries the sound of a deliverance feast. The call to praise from sunrise to sunset also supplies the sweep of the heavenly crowd.

Loud voices announce that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of the Lord, and the elders say He has begun to reign. Chapter 19:6 repeats the same announcement after the last great obstacle, Babylon, is gone, so the reign proclaimed at the seventh trumpet is now seen in its public effect.

The prophet rejoices in garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness and compares them to a bridegroom's and a bride's jewels. The verse shows that the clothing of the redeemed is a gift of God before it is a mark of the saint, and it prepares the sentence in Revelation 19:8, 'She was given.'

God covers Jerusalem's nakedness, bathes her, clothes her in fine linen and adorns her until she is renowned. The wedding of Revelation 19 is where that story lands for a people who in Ezekiel's day squandered the gift. The linen in both places is a gift from the husband.

The LORD says He will betroth His people to Himself forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and faithfulness. The marriage of the Lamb is the fulfilment of the promise, and the qualities Hosea lists are the character of the groom and the character the bride is clothed with.

Jesus's parable of the wedding banquet for a king's son includes invited guests who refuse, an open invitation to others, and a man without wedding clothes. It sheds light on verse 9: the invitation is real and the garment is necessary, and the king provides what the guests need to be at the feast.

Christ gave Himself for the church to sanctify her and present her to Himself without stain or wrinkle. The pattern of the Lamb's wedding is spelled out: He prepares the bride by His own sacrifice, and her purity at the feast is the result of that cleansing, not something she brings.

God prepares a banquet on His mountain for all peoples, swallows up death and wipes away every tear. The marriage supper is the full form of this feast, which shows why the scene is joyful for the ones invited and why Revelation can say the supper is open to people from every nation.

John again falls at an angel's feet and receives the same refusal, with 'fellow servant' and 'Worship God' repeated. The echo shows how strong the temptation is and how essential the lesson, and it shows that the book is held within a frame of worship reserved for God alone.

Peter lifts Cornelius from his knees and says he is only a man himself. The refusal in Acts and the refusal in Revelation 19:10 are two examples of the same rule, that the messengers of God redirect worship to the One who sent them, not to themselves.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a wedding of sorts. A man and a woman are brought together in a garden, and Genesis 2:24 calls it a union of one flesh, a verse Paul says is about Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31 and 5:32. The fall breaks that union, and the rest of the story is God courting a people who will not stay true. Israel's history is the story of a bride who is rescued, covered, and then lured away, as Ezekiel 16 and Hosea 1 to 3 show. The prophets' answer is a promise: God will betroth His people to Himself forever.

Revelation 19 is where that promise lands. It sits at the hinge between the fall of the harlot and the arrival of the rider on the white horse. The wedding is announced before the battle is shown, because the joy is certain even while the final conflict is pending. The chapter therefore does not describe a person's afterthought but the purpose of the whole redemption. The Lamb was slain to win a bride, and the point of the cross was not only forgiveness but union.

Looking back, the passage answers the desire of the martyrs under the altar, Revelation 6:9 to 11, who asked how long. It answers the hunger of the poor and the grief of the exiled, who were told that God would one day wipe away tears at a feast, Isaiah 25:6 to 8. It answers the silence that fell on Babylon in 18:22 and 18:23.

Looking forward, verse 9's blessing leads into the book's final chapters. The bride, called the wife of the Lamb, is shown as a city in Revelation 21:9 and 21:10, and the Spirit and the bride together say 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The marriage is the moment of arrival, and the new creation is the home in which the marriage is lived. The union begun in Eden and shattered by the serpent is restored in a better garden city, where God dwells with His people and 'they will be His people, and God Himself will be with them,' Revelation 21:3.

Between now and then, the church lives as the betrothed. She is clothed, invited and warned. She is called to prepare and to hold to the testimony of Jesus. And because the story ends with a wedding and not with a courtroom, the church can read the pains of the present as the final hours before the feast.

sermon.title: The Wedding Feast of the Lamb
sermon.why: Preaching directly on Revelation 19:1-10, Keller traces the single story of the Bible to its resolution in this vision, working through the prostitute and the problem, the Lamb and the solution, and the bride and the result, showing how every plotline of history is tied up in Jesus.

quiz.q: What does heaven's chorus in verses 1 to 3 celebrate?

options.text: God's true and just judgment on the great prostitute who corrupted the earth and shed His servants' blood.
options.note: Verse 2 states this explicitly as the reason for the praise.

options.text: The fall of a wealthy, seductive city, without reference to why it fell.
options.note: The city's fall is in view, but the text roots the praise in God's just judgment, not the ruin by itself.

options.text: The arrival of the thousand year reign described later in the book.
options.note: That scene comes in chapter 20; this chorus responds to Babylon's judgment.

options.text: The coronation of the beast as king over the earth.
options.note: The beast is judged elsewhere in Revelation, never celebrated; this chorus praises God.

quiz.q: What is the bride given to wear, and what does it represent, according to verses 7 and 8?

options.text: Fine linen, bright and pure, which the text identifies as the righteous acts of the saints.
options.note: Verse 8 states this directly.

options.text: Fine linen she wove entirely by her own effort, apart from any gift.
options.note: The text says she was given the clothing, pointing to grace as the source, even though the linen pictures real deeds.

options.text: Royal purple, symbolizing worldly wealth and status.
options.note: The color named is not purple but fine linen, bright and pure.

options.text: Sackcloth, symbolizing mourning and repentance.
options.note: The scene is one of joy and readiness, not mourning.

quiz.q: What happens when John falls at the angel's feet to worship him in verse 10?

options.text: The angel refuses worship, calls himself a fellow servant, and tells John to worship God instead.
options.note: This is exactly what the angel says in verse 10.

options.text: The angel accepts the worship gladly as heaven's chief messenger.
options.note: The opposite happens; the angel firmly refuses.

options.text: The angel says nothing and simply continues speaking.
options.note: The angel responds directly and pointedly to John's action.

options.text: The angel rebukes John for being present in the vision at all.
options.note: The rebuke concerns the act of worship, not John's presence.

quiz.q: According to verse 10, what is called 'the spirit of prophecy'?

options.text: The testimony of Jesus.
options.note: The verse states this directly: the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

options.text: The words of the twenty-four elders.
options.note: The elders appear earlier in the chapter, but this phrase is tied to the testimony of Jesus.

options.text: The book of the law given through Moses.
options.note: The verse does not mention the law here; it names the testimony of Jesus.

options.text: The angel's own personal message.
options.note: The angel points away from himself to the testimony of Jesus.

quiz.q: Who is pronounced blessed in verse 9?

options.text: Those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.
options.note: This is the exact wording of the beatitude in verse 9.

options.text: Those who host and prepare the marriage supper.
options.note: The blessing falls on the invited guests, not on those preparing the feast.

options.text: The twenty-four elders alone.
options.note: The elders are mentioned earlier in the chapter, but the beatitude names those invited, more broadly.

options.text: The servants of the great prostitute.
options.note: Her servants are not in view here; the blessing is on those invited to the Lamb's supper.

questions: Heaven bursts into Hallelujah over God's true and just judgment. Is there an injustice in your own life or in the world that you find hard to trust God with? What would it look like to let this scene shape your prayers about it?
The bride is given her fine linen; she does not weave it herself. Where are you tempted to think your standing with God depends on your own effort rather than on what He has given you in Christ?

The same linen is called the righteous acts of the saints, real deeds done by real people. How does knowing your good works flow from grace, rather than earning it, change how you go about doing them this week?
John falls to worship the angel almost by reflex, and is firmly redirected. What things, good things even, do you find your heart drifting toward worshiping instead of God?

Those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb are called blessed. How does picturing your future as an invitation to a wedding feast, rather than merely an escape from judgment, change the way you long for Christ's return?

translationNotes.note: Hallelujah transliterates the Hebrew hallelu Yah, praise the LORD. This is its only appearance anywhere in the New Testament, and it occurs four times within these six verses, a concentrated burst found nowhere else in Scripture's Greek text.
The great prostitute refers back to Babylon, described at length in chapters 17 and 18; the judgment celebrated here is the direct sequel to her fall.

Has made herself ready uses a verb that can carry the sense of readiness achieved, yet verse 8 immediately clarifies that even her clothing was given to her, holding together human readiness and divine gift.

The righteous acts of the saints translates dikaiomata, a different Greek word from dikaiosyne, the righteousness credited to believers by faith; this word names actual deeds, the visible fruit that grace produces.

meta.notes: BSB text supplied and pre-verified this session for Revelation 19:1-10. Straight quotation marks in the supplied text were rendered as curly quotation marks to match this repository's typographic convention; no wording was altered.
